doc.title: Bob Havens interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: How Dixieland has stayed the same, festivals and tuba versus string bass
summary: Havens describes Dixieland's history and instrument roles, the Sacramento festival, and his preference for string bass over banjo and tuba.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: The music that you were playing then, do you think it was similar or has it changed from King Oliver’s and Louis Armstrong’s, early on in jazz.

Well I think Dixieland primarily is still the same type of music that it was. It was considered the first type of jazz music. Well first at the turn of the century was I guess what you’d call ragtime music, which was mostly played on the piano. Then the Dixieland bands started out with the Original Dixieland band out of New Orleans, and basically it was played then just about the same as it is now. But there is some influence between other styles of music that have sort of gotten into the simple Dixieland style. Modern jazz sort of came along — well first we had Dixieland, like World War I and on the way through, and then in the first part of the thirties, I guess the Swing era started to come through with the Benny Goodman and the big bands. And the Dixieland influence I think has always been there no matter what style it is. There’s that simple influence that most musicians tend to learn before they go into anything else.
This particular festival is not oriented toward Dixieland too much.
Do you make the other ones that are?

Yes. Well I don’t know. The biggest — well the festival that is considered the largest in the country is considered a Dixieland festival and that’s the one in Sacramento. And I was there when it started out, in 1974 I think. It was directed towards the Dixieland style groups, small groups. And I think it has grown into the largest festival in existence of that style. And it still is presented in such a way that the trumpet generally carries the simple lead and the trombone generally plays bass notes or a little more ambitious than the bass, which is the job of the trombone player in a Dixieland band. And the clarinet plays the obbligato above the melody, and that’s pretty much the way they still play it. It’s a simple type of music.
Right. Most of those bands use tubas instead of bass players?

Yeah. It started out, well back in the twenties I guess, the string bass just never quite carried very well on recordings, the old primitive, acoustical recordings. The string bass didn’t carry so the tuba seemed to have a little more power on recordings and so they used that. But in later years I think the string bass became just about as popular as the tuba with the small band. And I personally prefer a string bass in my band when I have one. I like the string bass and the piano. But there are other groups that — some would consider purists. The purists go back to the days when they used mostly banjos and tubas. That seems to be two instruments that go together. Now it was never one of my favorite combinations. So I lean towards the other direction.
